title: FULL OUTER JOIN
objective: Use FULL OUTER JOIN to keep unmatched rows from both tables, classify each row as matched / left-only / right-only, and COALESCE keys from both sides.
context: The data-quality lead is running reconciliations: does the supplier master agree with the product catalogue? do customers and orders line up? Mismatches on EITHER side matter, so neither table may be the 'driving' one.

exercises.title: Supplier–product reconciliation
exercises.question: Procurement wants one list containing every supplier AND every product, matched where possible.
exercises.prompt: Return supplier_id (from suppliers), supplier_name, product_id and product_name for every supplier and every product: matched pairs, suppliers with no products (product columns NULL) and products with no matching supplier (supplier columns NULL).
hints: Unmatched rows from BOTH sides must survive.
FULL OUTER JOIN (or FULL JOIN) on supplier_id.
SELECT s.supplier_id, s.supplier_name, p.product_id, p.product_name FROM suppliers s FULL OUTER JOIN products p ON p.supplier_id = s.supplier_id;
exercises.why: Reconciliation reports need both kinds of gap at once — master data without activity and activity without master data.

recall.q: How do you compute the row count of a FULL OUTER JOIN?
recall.a: Matched rows + unmatched left rows + unmatched right rows.

exercises.join_notes: suppliers 5, products 25. Result: 26 rows = 23 matched pairs (suppliers 1–3 repeat 6 times, supplier 4 five times) + 1 supplier-only row (5 'Andes Trading', product columns NULL) + 2 product-only rows (21 'Water Bottle' whose supplier 9 doesn't exist, 22 'Phone Stand' with NULL supplier_id — both with supplier_id and supplier_name NULL). INNER would give 23, suppliers LEFT JOIN products 24, products LEFT JOIN suppliers 25.

exercises.title: Only the mismatches, classified
exercises.question: Data quality wants just the problem rows from the supplier–product reconciliation, with a label.
exercises.prompt: Return supplier_id (= COALESCE(s.supplier_id, p.supplier_id)), product_id and issue, only for unmatched rows. issue is 'supplier has no products' when the product side is missing, 'product has no supplier_id' when the product's supplier_id is NULL, and 'unknown supplier' when the product's supplier_id points to no supplier.
hints: Unmatched = one side's primary key is NULL. Filter with WHERE s.supplier_id IS NULL OR p.product_id IS NULL.
Order the CASE branches: product side missing → p.supplier_id NULL → otherwise unknown supplier.

SELECT COALESCE(s.supplier_id, p.supplier_id) AS supplier_id, p.product_id, CASE WHEN p.product_id IS NULL THEN ... END AS issue FROM suppliers s FULL OUTER JOIN products p ON ... WHERE s.supplier_id IS NULL OR p.product_id IS NULL
exercises.why: An exception report — only the rows that need action — is what data stewards actually work from.

recall.a: In a FULL JOIN either side can be NULL; COALESCE shows whichever key exists (5 from suppliers, 9 from products).

exercises.join_notes: The FULL JOIN yields 26 rows (23 matched + 1 + 2); the WHERE keeps the 3 unmatched ones: supplier 5 (no products), product 21 with supplier_id 9 (unknown supplier — COALESCE shows the 9 from the product side) and product 22 (supplier_id NULL even after COALESCE, because it is NULL on both sides). Here a WHERE on NULLs is deliberate: we WANT only the NULL-padded rows.

exercises.title: Customers without orders and orders without customers
exercises.question: Finance and CRM want one exception list: customers who never ordered and orders that belong to no known customer.
exercises.prompt: Return customer_id (= COALESCE(c.customer_id, o.customer_id)), customer_name (customers.name) and order_id for rows of a FULL OUTER JOIN of customers and orders where either side is unmatched.
hints: Both directions matter → FULL OUTER JOIN.
Unmatched rows: c.customer_id IS NULL (order-only) OR o.order_id IS NULL (customer-only).
SELECT COALESCE(c.customer_id, o.customer_id) AS customer_id, c.name AS customer_name, o.order_id FROM customers c FULL OUTER JOIN orders o ON ... WHERE c.customer_id IS NULL OR o.order_id IS NULL
exercises.why: One query, both failure modes. This is the backbone of source-to-target reconciliation in data engineering.

recall.q: In this result, why is customer_name NULL for customer 99?
recall.a: Customer 99 exists only as a value in orders; there is no customers row, so all customers columns are NULL-padded.

exercises.join_notes: customers 20, orders 60. The FULL JOIN returns 63 rows = 59 matched (customer rows repeated once per order) + 3 customer-only rows (18, 19, 20; order_id NULL) + 1 order-only row (order 31, customer 99; customer_name NULL). The WHERE keeps those 4 exceptions. Neither a LEFT nor a RIGHT JOIN alone can show both kinds.

exercises.title: Reconciliation scorecard
exercises.question: The data-quality dashboard wants three numbers summarising how customers and orders line up.
exercises.prompt: Return a single row with matched_rows (rows of the FULL OUTER JOIN of customers and orders where both sides exist), customers_without_orders and orders_without_customer.
hints: Classify each FULL JOIN row with CASE, then SUM the 1s.
Test the primary keys: o.order_id IS NULL → customer-only; c.customer_id IS NULL → order-only.
SUM(CASE WHEN o.order_id IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS customers_without_orders, ...
exercises.why: Monitoring jobs run exactly this query nightly and alert when the unmatched counts move.

recall.q: Why test o.order_id and not o.customer_id for 'customer without orders'?
recall.a: o.order_id is the PK of orders and is NULL only on NULL-padded rows; o.customer_id could be NULL in real data too.

exercises.join_notes: The FULL JOIN has 63 rows: matched_rows = 59 (orders that found their customer; customers with many orders count many times — that's the one-to-many multiplication), customers_without_orders = 3 (18, 19, 20) and orders_without_customer = 1 (order 31 → customer 99). 59 + 3 + 1 = 63, and 59 + 1 = 60 orders, 17 + 3 = 20 customers — the reconciliation balances.

exercises.title: 2024 vs. 2025 orders per customer (FULL JOIN of aggregates)
exercises.question: Growth wants to compare each customer's order count in 2024 with 2025 — including customers active in only one of the years.
exercises.prompt: Build two per-customer aggregates from orders (any status): orders in 2024 and orders in 2025 (use strftime('%Y', order_date)). FULL OUTER JOIN them on customer_id and return customer_id, orders_2024 and orders_2025 (0 when the customer had no orders that year), one row per customer_id that ordered in either year (include customer_id 99 — it is in orders).
hints: Aggregate first (one row per customer per year), THEN join — joining one-row-per-customer sets can't multiply.
Customers active in only one year must survive from either side → FULL OUTER JOIN; COALESCE the key and the counts.

WITH y2024 AS (SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS n FROM orders WHERE strftime('%Y', order_date) = '2024' GROUP BY customer_id), y2025 AS (...) SELECT COALESCE(a.customer_id, b.customer_id) AS customer_id, COALESCE(a.n,0) AS orders_2024, COALESCE(b.n,0) AS orders_2025 FROM y2024 a FULL OUTER JOIN y2025 b ON ...
exercises.why: Period-over-period comparisons (retained / churned / new) are a FULL JOIN of two aggregates — the classic cohort building block.

recall.q: Which customers would an INNER JOIN of the two yearly aggregates lose?
recall.a: Everyone active in only one year — churned (2024 only) and new (2025 only) customers.

exercises.join_notes: The 2024 aggregate has 12 customer rows (1–12), the 2025 aggregate 16 (15 real customers + 99). Both are one row per customer, so the join cannot multiply rows. Result: 18 rows = 10 customers in both years + 2 only in 2024 (customers 5 and 8 — churned; orders_2025 NULL → 0) + 6 only in 2025 (13, 14, 15, 16, 17 and the orphan 99 — orders_2024 NULL → 0). Without COALESCE on the key, the 2025-only rows would show customer_id NULL.
exercises.snowflake: Identical in Snowflake; YEAR(order_date) = 2024 is the idiomatic filter there.

exercises.title: Category tree vs. product categories
exercises.question: The catalogue team maintains a category tree; merchandising tags products with a category text. Do they agree?
exercises.prompt: Aggregate products by category (product count per category value, NULL category included as its own group). FULL OUTER JOIN that to categories on category_name = category and return category_id (from categories; NULL if not in the tree), category_name (COALESCE of the tree name and the product category) and product_count (0 when no product uses that category).
hints: Aggregate products to one row per category first (a CTE), so the join stays one-to-one.
Neither side drives — tree nodes without products and product categories missing from the tree both matter.
FROM categories c FULL OUTER JOIN product_cats pc ON pc.category = c.category_name, COALESCE the name and the count
exercises.why: Taxonomy drift between a master hierarchy and tagged data is a constant source of 'Other / Unknown' buckets in dashboards.

recall.q: Product 20 has a NULL category. Why does it show up as an unmatched row?
recall.a: NULL = 'anything' (even NULL) is never true, so the NULL group can't match any tree node.

exercises.join_notes: categories has 14 rows; the product aggregate has 6 (Electronics 7, Home 6, Apparel 4, Books 3, Sports 4, NULL 1). Result: 15 rows = 5 matched top-level categories + 9 tree-only nodes (All Products, Audio, Computer Accessories, Kitchen, Decor, Footwear, Outerwear, Fitness, Strength Training; product_count 0) + 1 product-only row: the NULL category of product 20, with category_id NULL and category_name NULL. NULL never equals NULL, so it cannot match. No multiplication: both sides are one row per category.

worked_example.question: Classify every supplier/product row as matched, supplier-only or product-only and count them.
worked_example.sql:
SELECT CASE WHEN s.supplier_id IS NULL THEN 'product without supplier'
            WHEN p.product_id  IS NULL THEN 'supplier without products'
            ELSE 'matched' END AS match_status,
       COUNT(*) AS row_count
FROM suppliers AS s
FULL OUTER JOIN products AS p ON p.supplier_id = s.supplier_id
GROUP BY match_status
ORDER BY match_status;
worked_example.explanation: 23 matched pairs, 2 products without a valid supplier (21 and 22) and 1 supplier without products (5) = 26 rows. An INNER JOIN would show only the 23; LEFT from suppliers 24; LEFT from products 25.

recipe:
**The join recipe — do it in this order, every time, before typing SQL**

1. **Pick the driving table.** Which table's rows is the answer *about*? ("every customer…", "each order line…")
   That table goes first, after `FROM` — it is the **left table**.
2. **Name the right table(s) and the shared key.** What column links them? Is it PK → FK (one-to-many) or
   one-to-one? Which side is the "many" side?
3. **Ask: "must every row of the left table survive, even with no match?"**
   - no → `INNER JOIN` (unmatched rows silently disappear)
   - yes → `LEFT JOIN` (unmatched rows stay, right-side columns become NULL)
   - rows from *both* sides must survive → `FULL OUTER JOIN`
4. **Predict the row count before you run it.** Count the inputs (`SELECT COUNT(*) …`), think about
   matches per row (0, 1 or many), write your guess down — then run and compare. A surprise means
   you misunderstood the grain, the key or the data.

**FULL OUTER JOIN = LEFT JOIN ∪ RIGHT JOIN.** Every row of both tables survives: matched pairs once,
left-only rows with NULL right columns, right-only rows with NULL left columns.

```sql
SELECT COALESCE(s.supplier_id, p.supplier_id) AS supplier_id,   -- key from whichever side exists
       s.supplier_name, p.product_id,
       CASE WHEN s.supplier_id IS NULL THEN 'product only'
            WHEN p.product_id  IS NULL THEN 'supplier only'
            ELSE 'matched' END AS match_status
FROM   suppliers AS s
FULL OUTER JOIN products AS p ON p.supplier_id = s.supplier_id;
-- predict: matched pairs + left-only + right-only = 23 + 1 + 2 = 26
```

- **Row count = matched rows + unmatched left rows + unmatched right rows.** Predict each piece.
- Classify rows by testing each side's **primary key** for NULL.
- Use `COALESCE(left.key, right.key)` for a single key column — either side may be NULL.
- Filters on either table in WHERE remove NULL-padded rows → put them in ON or pre-filter in a subquery/CTE.
- Great pattern: FULL JOIN two *aggregated* sets (2024 vs 2025 per customer) and COALESCE the measures to 0.
- (Older MySQL lacks FULL JOIN: emulate with LEFT JOIN UNION RIGHT anti-join. SQLite ≥ 3.39 and Snowflake support it.)
common_mistakes: Selecting the key from only one side (s.supplier_id) — it is NULL on the other side's unmatched rows; use COALESCE.
Adding a WHERE on one table's column, which removes the other side's NULL-padded rows (FULL becomes LEFT/RIGHT/INNER).
FULL JOINing two detail tables when you meant to compare aggregates — aggregate first, then join one-row-per-key sets.
Forgetting COALESCE(measure, 0) — unmatched sides give NULL, which breaks arithmetic like orders_2025 - orders_2024.
Expecting NULL keys to match each other — they never do.
recall: How do you tell a left-only row from a right-only row?
Check which side's primary key is NULL.
Why COALESCE the join key in the SELECT list of a FULL JOIN?
Because either side's key can be NULL; COALESCE returns the one that exists.
review_next: Lesson 14 chains three or more tables. The rule doesn't change: one join at a time, one row-count prediction at a time.
